title: Runtime extension surface stability and versioning contract
author: Maya Chen
body:
Summary

This document defines the stability, compatibility, and versioning contract for any extensions to the Redwood serving runtime extension surface. "Extensions" in this document include kernel plugins, priority/admission hooks, observability adapters, custom scheduling policies, and lightweight binary-compatible runtime modules. The goal is to enable third-party and internal teams to safely integrate new features while preserving customer-facing SLOs, rollout safety, and fast rollback paths.

Scope

- Applies to all code and artifacts that are loaded dynamically into the serving runtime process (ld.so, plugin loader, dynamic shared objects), as well as to external modules that register callbacks with the runtime over the internal plugin API (rpc or in-process).
- Does NOT apply to model files, model weights, or user prompts. It DOES apply to model-serving kernel implementations and dispatch adapters.

Goals

1. Prevent runtime crashes and silent performance regressions after extension deploys.
2. Provide a clear ABI/semantic compatibility guarantee across minor releases so teams can plan integration windows.
3. Define test and rollout requirements that keep production SLOs (p50 latency, p99 latency, availability, error budget) within agreed thresholds.
4. Provide an explicit deprecation and sunset path for unstable extension APIs.

Compatibility model

We use a three-tier compatibility model for the extension surface:

- Strict ABI compatibility (patch releases): binary-compatible, no symbol or struct layout changes. Backward-compatible behavior guaranteed. Extensions built against a patch-level release must run without recompilation.

- Semantic compatibility (minor releases): may add optional fields, new callback hooks, and extension-facing feature flags. Extensions built against an older minor release should continue to function with feature-gates disabled. If an extension requires new hooks, it must declare an explicit minimum minor version.

- Breaking changes (major releases): may change core interfaces and require a rebuild of extensions. Major releases are accompanied by a migration guide and a six-month opt-in dual-run period (see Rollout & Migration section).

Versioning policy and manifest

Every runtime artifact (core runtime, kernel plugins, adapters) must ship with a manifest file: runtime-extension-manifest.yaml

Example manifest:

---
name: fast-kernel-plugin
version: 1.2.0
build_target: rwinference-x86_64-gpu-v2
abi_hash: 2f7a4b8e
min_runtime_minor: 2
capabilities:
  - kernel:sharded-attention
  - telemetry:streaming-metrics
allowed_flags:
  - "enable_experimental_prefetch"
signature: "sha256:..."
---

Rules:

- version follows semver: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Runtime core only increments MAJOR when ABI/semantic breaks are necessary.
- abi_hash is a build-time hash of exported symbols and public struct layout. Runtime will refuse to load a plugin if abi_hash mismatches unless explicit override is provided and an operator acknowledges risk.
- min_runtime_minor indicates the minimum runtime minor version that provides required optional hooks.

Extension lifecycle and stability labels

Extensions must be labeled for expected stability in their manifest: alpha | beta | stable

- alpha: experimental; allowed only in sandbox and canary clusters, never in global production regions.
- beta: allowed in limited production audiences after automated safety tests pass. Beta may be promoted to stable after 2 months with no regression signals.
- stable: cleared for general production rollout.

Integration and preflight checklist (required before canary rollout)

1. Automated build and signature verification:
   - Build in CI with reproducible output.
   - Provide signed manifest and signature verification steps.
2. Local microbenchmarks:
   - Run the per-token microbenchmark suite with a representative request corpus (see Benchmarking section).
   - Compare per-token CPU/GPU time; threshold: no >5% regression in median token processing time for kernels, and no >10% regression in p99 latency for end-to-end small requests.
3. Telemetry smoke tests:
   - Verify telemetry adapters emit the runtime-defined trace events and do not create cyclical logging.
4. Safety fuzz tests:
   - Run simulated malformed frames, OOM scenarios, and sequential plugin unload/reload to ensure stability.
5. SLO simulation: 
   - Run the synthetic traffic simulator (operational-workload-simulator) with the extension enabled and confirm p99 latency and availability stay within the attack budget for the target fleet.

Rollout & migration procedure

1. Canary: gate to a single canary cluster that hosts <1% of traffic by default. Monitor for 1 hour of steady-state and one traffic spike test.
2. Regional ramp: expand to a single region at 5% with automated rollback triggers on:
   - increase in p99 latency >10% vs baseline for 10 minutes,
   - error rate increase >0.5% absolute,
   - kernel crash or SIGSEGV in plugin.
3. Controlled ramp: 25% -> 50% -> 100% with progressive verification and a 24-hour hold at each step for stable labels.
4. Emergency rollback: operator runbook and an automated controller exist to yank the extension from active nodes and revert kernel routing to a safe fallback variant. See Runbook section for CLI commands.

Measurement and SLO impact accounting

- Any extension that modifies request-path kernels must publish an anticipated SLO delta in the manifest and in the PR.
- Runtime CI will run a differential benchmark comparing baseline and extension to generate a per-route cost and latency delta table. This table becomes part of the rollout ticket and product release notes.

Telemetry and observability contract

Extensions must emit the following minimal signals to integrate with runtime observability:

- extension.loaded (gauge) with fields: name, version, stability_label
- extension.hook.latency_ms (histogram) for each registered callback
- extension.error (counter) with categorized error types (init, hook-failure, oom)
- optional: extension.span (trace) linking to request.trace_id when executing in-path

Example tracing header (JSON):
{
  "extension": "fast-kernel-plugin",
  "version": "1.2.0",
  "span_id": "...",
  "trace_id": "..."
}

Runtime load-time checks and policy enforcement

At process start and plugin load time the runtime performs:

1. manifest signature verification (fail-fast if missing and not in debug environment)
2. abi_hash check and capability whitelist enforcement
3. capability vs policy check: certain capabilities (e.g., direct GPU memory management) require explicit operator allowance and are disallowed in shared multitenant fleets by default

Policy table (operator-managed):

| Capability | Default allowed in shared fleet | Requires operator consent | Comments |
| GPU direct memory | false | true | High risk: can cause cross-tenant OOM
| telemetry:streaming-metrics | true | false | Low risk
| kernel:sharded-attention | false | true | Requires isolation tests

Runbook: emergency disable and rollback (quick commands)

1. Mark plugin unschedulable via service registry:
   - redwoodctl runtime plugin disable fast-kernel-plugin --cluster canary
2. Trigger rolling restart of nodes that loaded plugin (graceful drain):
   - redwoodctl node drain --label plugin:fast-kernel-plugin --grace-period 120s
3. If crash loop persists, flip the runtime feature-flag fallback:
   - redwoodctl runtime set-flag --name enforce-plugin-fallback --value true

Testing and benchmark suite guidance

- Use the per-token microbenchmark and the request-surface replay (see benchmarking-and-perf-suite). Capture: median token time, p95/p99 end-to-end latency, GPU occupancy, and allocator fragmentation.
- For kernel-level changes, include unit tests that validate KV cache behavior, prefetch ordering, and cooperative preemption interactions.

Example microbenchmark invocation:

./bench/run_per_token.sh --plugin ./fast-kernel-plugin.so --corpus small-oral-requests.json --warmup 60 --measure 300

Deprecation and sunset policy

- Stable extension APIs can be deprecated with at least one minor runtime release notice (minimum 90 days). Deprecation must include: migration guide, compatibility shim if feasible, and test plans.
- Sunset: if an API is to be removed, provide 6 months notice with automated compatibility checks and an extended canary window.

Ownership and escalation

- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime team (oncall rotation).
- Secondary: eng-platform (release automation), eng-infra (operator policy).
- Escalation contact: runtime-oncall@redwood.ai and platform-ops@redwood.ai.

Appendices

A. Sample minimal CI job steps:
1. build plugin -> produce artifact + signature
2. run unit tests and fuzz harness
3. run microbench suite and compare against baseline metric file
4. publish to internal artifact registry with manifest

B. Migration example (from runtime minor 2 -> 3):
- If your plugin uses the new hook on_request_prefetch introduced in minor 3, set min_runtime_minor: 3 and provide runtime fallback path that skips the hook when absent.
